_about: IPCC reports by year, with their main messages. Messages are paraphrased from each report's Summary for Policymakers and checked against published summaries; quotation marks show the IPCC's own words. Edit freely.
about: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change does not publish every year: it works in cycles of six to eight years, each producing three working group reports and a synthesis, with special reports in between. This list has every assessment report and the special reports most relevant to energy.

reports.title: First Assessment Report (FAR)
reports.attribution: Warming so far 'could be largely due to natural variability'; clear detection not expected for a decade or more.
messages: Emissions from human activities are substantially increasing the concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which will warm the Earth's surface.
Global mean temperature rose 0.3 to 0.6 °C over the previous 100 years.
With business as usual, warming of about 0.3 °C per decade during the 21st century (range 0.2 to 0.5).
Sea level would rise about 6 cm per decade, reaching about 65 cm by 2100.
Stabilising concentrations of long-lived gases at 1990 levels would need emission cuts of more than 60%.
reports.energy: CO2 from fossil fuels is identified as responsible for over half of the enhanced greenhouse effect.
reports.impact: The scientific basis for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, agreed at Rio in 1992.

reports.title: Second Assessment Report (SAR): Climate Change 1995
reports.attribution: 'The balance of evidence suggests a discernible human influence on global climate.'
messages: First statement that a human signal can be seen in the climate record, with the caveat that the ability to quantify it is limited.
Temperature has risen 0.3 to 0.6 °C since the late 19th century; the trend is unlikely to be entirely natural.
CO2 remains the most important contributor to human-caused warming.
Many aspects of climate change are effectively irreversible because of the long timescales involved.
reports.energy: Introduced the question of which concentration level counts as 'dangerous', which later became temperature targets and carbon budgets.
reports.impact: Informed the negotiation of the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997.

reports.title: Third Assessment Report (TAR): Climate Change 2001
reports.attribution: 'New and stronger evidence that most of the warming observed over the last 50 years is attributable to human activities' (likely, more than 66%).
messages: Global average surface temperature rose about 0.6 °C over the 20th century.
Projected warming of 1.4 to 5.8 °C between 1990 and 2100, depending on the emissions scenario.
Projected sea level rise of 0.1 to 0.9 m over the same period.
reports.energy: The wide warming range comes mainly from different emission scenarios (the SRES family), which made energy choices the central uncertainty.
reports.impact: Shaped the implementation rules of the Kyoto Protocol and brought the scenario approach into policy debate.

reports.title: Fourth Assessment Report (AR4): Climate Change 2007
reports.attribution: Warming is 'unequivocal'; most of the warming since the mid-20th century is 'very likely' (more than 90%) due to human greenhouse gas emissions.
messages: Warming of about 0.74 °C over the last 100 years.
Projected warming by 2100 from 1.8 °C (range 1.1 to 2.9) in the lowest scenario to 4.0 °C (2.4 to 6.4) in the highest, relative to 1980-1999.
Climate sensitivity likely between 2 and 4.5 °C per doubling of CO2, best estimate about 3 °C.
Sea level rise of 18 to 59 cm by 2100, not counting possible rapid changes in ice flow.
Stabilising at 445 to 535 ppm CO2-equivalent would cost less than 3% of global GDP, slowing annual growth by less than 0.12 percentage points.
reports.energy: First assessment to conclude that deep emission cuts are affordable with known and emerging technologies.
reports.impact: The IPCC shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore; the report framed the Bali roadmap and the Copenhagen negotiations.

reports.title: Special Report on Renewable Energy Sources and Climate Change Mitigation (SRREN)
messages: Renewables supplied about 13% of global primary energy in 2008, most of it traditional biomass.
Reviewed 164 scenarios; in the most ambitious, renewables supply close to 80% of world energy by 2050.
The technical potential of renewables is far larger than demand; the limits are cost, integration and policy, not resources.
reports.energy: The IPCC's only report devoted to energy supply technologies. Its cost figures for solar and wind are long out of date: both fell far faster than it expected.
reports.impact: Established that a mostly renewable energy system is technically possible, which later scenario work built on.

reports.title: Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)
reports.attribution: 'It is extremely likely (more than 95%) that human influence has been the dominant cause of the observed warming since the mid-20th century.'
messages: Warming depends on cumulative CO2 emissions: this is the origin of the 'carbon budget'. Warming continues to be locked in even if emissions stop.
CO2 concentrations are at levels unprecedented in at least 800,000 years; the ocean has absorbed about 90% of the added heat.
Without new policies, warming of 3.7 to 4.8 °C by 2100 (median range).
Pledges at the time were broadly consistent with staying below 3 °C, not 2 °C.
Delaying emission cuts makes reaching any target more expensive.
reports.energy: In pathways that hold warming to 2 °C, the share of low-carbon electricity (renewables, nuclear, carbon capture) rises from about 30% to more than 80% by 2050.
reports.impact: The scientific foundation of the Paris Agreement (2015) and its 'well below 2 °C' goal.

reports.title: Special Report: Global Warming of 1.5 °C (SR1.5)
messages: Human activities had already caused about 1.0 °C of warming (0.8 to 1.2).
At the current rate, 1.5 °C is likely to be reached between 2030 and 2052.
Limiting warming to 1.5 °C needs CO2 emissions to fall about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050.
Half a degree matters: coral reefs decline 70-90% at 1.5 °C and more than 99% at 2 °C; an ice-free Arctic summer once a century versus once a decade.
Pledges at the time pointed to about 3 °C by 2100.
reports.energy: Made 'net zero by 2050' the organising target for energy policy and for scenarios such as the IEA's Net Zero Emissions pathway.
reports.impact: Requested by governments in the Paris Agreement; it triggered the wave of national and corporate net-zero pledges.

reports.title: Special Report on Climate Change and Land (SRCCL)
messages: Human use directly affects more than 70% of the ice-free land surface.
Agriculture, forestry and other land use account for roughly a quarter of human greenhouse gas emissions.
25 to 30% of food produced is lost or wasted.
Land is both a source and a sink of carbon; better land management can help, but land cannot do everything at once.
reports.energy: Warns against relying on very large areas of bioenergy crops (including bioenergy with carbon capture), because they compete with food and ecosystems. This limits a technology many 1.5 °C scenarios lean on.
reports.impact: Put food systems and land competition on the climate-policy agenda.

reports.title: Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC)
messages: The ocean has taken up more than 90% of the excess heat in the climate system since 1970, and the rate of ocean warming has more than doubled since 1993.
Sea level could rise about 30-60 cm by 2100 if warming stays well below 2 °C, and about 60-110 cm if emissions keep rising strongly.
Marine heatwaves have very likely doubled in frequency since 1982.
About 625 million people live in low-lying coastal areas.
reports.energy: Relevant to energy mainly through infrastructure risk: coastal power plants, ports and grids, and hydropower fed by glaciers and snow.
reports.impact: Raised the upper end of sea-level projections compared with AR5.

reports.title: Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), Working Group I: The Physical Science Basis
reports.attribution: 'It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.'
messages: Global surface temperature in 2011-2020 was about 1.1 °C above 1850-1900.
1.5 °C is likely to be reached before 2040 in all scenarios considered.
Remaining carbon budget from the start of 2020: about 500 GtCO2 for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C, 400 GtCO2 for a 67% chance.
Climate sensitivity narrowed to 2.5 to 4.0 °C per doubling of CO2, best estimate 3 °C.
Sea level likely to rise 0.5 to 1 m by 2100; 2 m cannot be ruled out.
reports.energy: Every tonne of CO2 adds to warming, so the remaining budget translates directly into how much fossil fuel can still be burned.
reports.impact: Released ahead of the Glasgow climate conference (COP26); the UN Secretary-General called it a 'code red for humanity'.

reports.title: AR6, Working Group II: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability
messages: At least 3.3 billion people, about 40% of the world population, live in conditions highly vulnerable to climate change.
Some impacts are already irreversible, and some limits to adaptation have been reached.
About one billion people in low-lying coastal areas face increasing flood risk by mid-century.
Effective conservation of roughly 30 to 50% of land, freshwater and ocean areas would help ecosystems cope.
reports.energy: Energy systems are themselves exposed: heat and drought reduce output from thermal and hydro plants and raise cooling demand.
reports.impact: Strengthened the case for adaptation finance and for the loss-and-damage fund agreed later in 2022.

reports.title: AR6, Working Group III: Mitigation of Climate Change
messages: To limit warming to 1.5 °C, global greenhouse gas emissions must peak before 2025 and fall 43% by 2030 compared with 2019.
From 2010 to 2019 the cost of solar electricity fell 85%, wind 55% and lithium-ion batteries 85%.
Options costing USD 100 per tonne of CO2 or less could halve global emissions by 2030.
Demand-side measures could cut emissions 40-70% by 2050.
Net-zero CO2 is reached around the early 2050s in 1.5 °C pathways and the early 2070s in 2 °C pathways; carbon removal is needed to balance emissions that are hard to eliminate.
reports.energy: The most important IPCC report for energy: chapter 6 covers energy systems and chapter 3 the scenario ensemble (both are in the Literature tab). Nuclear and carbon capture play widely varying roles across pathways.
reports.impact: Its finding that low-cost options could halve emissions by 2030 became a standard reference in energy policy.

reports.title: AR6 Synthesis Report: Climate Change 2023
reports.attribution: 'Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming.'
messages: Warming has reached 1.1 °C; there is a more than 50% chance of reaching 1.5 °C between 2021 and 2040.
For 1.5 °C, greenhouse gas emissions must fall 43% by 2030 and 60% by 2035 relative to 2019, with CO2 at net zero in the early 2050s.
Existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would emit about 850 GtCO2, well above the roughly 510 GtCO2 budget for 1.5 °C.
National pledges would cut emissions only about 7% by 2030.
Climate finance needs to rise three to six times by 2030; there is a 'rapidly closing window of opportunity'.
reports.energy: States plainly that the fossil plants already built or planned exceed the 1.5 °C budget unless they are retired early or fitted with carbon capture.
reports.impact: The scientific input to the first global stocktake under the Paris Agreement (COP28, 2023).

reports.title: Seventh Assessment Report (AR7) cycle
messages: Outlines of the three working group reports were agreed in February 2025; release dates are not yet fixed.
A Special Report on Climate Change and Cities is in preparation.
Two methodology reports are planned for 2027: one on short-lived climate forcers, one on carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
The Synthesis Report is planned for late 2029.
reports.energy: The methodology report on carbon removal and capture will set the accounting rules that decide how much these technologies can count in national inventories.
reports.impact: Governments have disagreed on whether the reports should be ready for the second global stocktake in 2028.
